records.sourceFile: In-season monitoring of hip and groin strength, health and function in elite youth soccer- Implementing an early detection and management strategy over two consecutive seasons.pdf

paper.citation: Wollin M, Thorborg K, Welvaert M, Pizzari T. In-season monitoring of hip and groin strength, health and function in elite youth soccer: Implementing an early detection and management strategy over two consecutive seasons. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2018;21(10):988-993.
paper.abstract: This longitudinal cohort study described an in-season hip and groin surveillance strategy in 27 elite male youth soccer players. Monthly adductor strength, adductor-to-abductor strength ratio, and HAGOS scores were compared with predefined alert thresholds to prompt further assessment.
paper.tldr: Monthly hip and groin monitoring generated frequent alerts and showed that group strength and self-reported function improved early in the season. The study demonstrates a workable surveillance process, but it does not validate the thresholds as injury-prediction or prevention rules.
paper.methods: Twenty-seven elite male youth players were followed across two seasons. Testing included adductor strength, adductor-to-abductor strength ratio, and six HAGOS subscales; alerts were triggered by greater than 15% strength loss, a ratio below 0.90, or a HAGOS subscale below 75.
paper.findings: The system generated 105 alerts involving 70% of players; 40% were strength related and 60% came from HAGOS. Adductor strength and strength ratio increased by month two, most HAGOS subscales improved at the first in-season time point, and 87% of time-loss events were minimal or mild.
paper.limitations: This was a small, single-program male youth cohort without a control group. Alert thresholds were operational choices rather than validated diagnostic or prognostic cut points, so the design cannot establish that monitoring prevented injury.
paper.practicalImplications: A repeatable monthly battery can help identify meaningful within-athlete changes and prompt targeted follow-up. Staff should evaluate trends alongside symptoms, exposure, clinical findings, and the athlete's own baseline rather than treating one threshold breach as a diagnosis.
paper.athleteDev: Use serial adductor strength and hip/groin function measures to guide individualized supplemental strength or load-management conversations. Preserve preseason and early-season baselines because rapid group improvement can make a single preseason value a poor long-term comparator.
paper.rtp: During groin reconditioning, serial strength ratios and HAGOS domains can document progress and flag setbacks. They should complement—not replace—clinical examination, sport-specific loading, and shared return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Chronic cannabis consumption and physical exercise performance in healthy adults - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Kramer A, Sinclair J, Sharpe L, Sarris J. Chronic cannabis consumption and physical exercise performance in healthy adults: A systematic review. Journal of Cannabis Research. 2020;2(1):34.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined chronic cannabis use and exercise-performance outcomes in healthy adults. Eight databases and forward searching produced four eligible studies assessing measures such as maximal oxygen uptake, physical work capacity, resting heart rate, blood pressure, and pulmonary function.
paper.tldr: Four small cross-sectional studies found no consistent difference in VO2max or physical work capacity between chronic cannabis users and non-users. That thin evidence base does not establish safety, recovery benefit, or absence of impairment with current products, doses, or acute use.
paper.methods: The authors searched eight databases through January 2020 for cross-sectional, longitudinal, or intervention studies relating chronic cannabis consumption to sports-performance outcomes. Four studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesized qualitatively.
paper.findings: Resting heart rate differed between groups in one study, while VO2max and physical work capacity did not differ consistently. The included studies did not directly evaluate recovery or endurance effects, and no ergogenic or ergolytic conclusion could be established.
paper.limitations: Only four studies were eligible, all with cross-sectional limitations and several with small samples or older, lower-potency exposure patterns. Exposure definitions varied, confounding was substantial, and causal effects cannot be inferred.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not interpret null group differences as evidence that cannabis improves recovery or is performance-neutral for an individual athlete. Decisions should account for acute impairment, health, policy, product composition, dose, and timing beyond the narrow chronic-use outcomes reviewed here.
paper.athleteDev: This review provides no basis for recommending cannabis as an ergogenic or recovery strategy. Education should distinguish unsupported performance claims from medical, behavioral, legal, and anti-doping considerations.
paper.rtp: No return-to-sport protocol or clearance evidence was studied. Cannabis use should not be used to infer readiness, symptom resolution, or safe participation.

records.sourceFile: Acute-chronic workload ratio and training monotony variations over the season in professional soccer - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Rico-González M, González Fernández FT, Oliveira R, Clemente FM. Acute:chronic workload ratio and training monotony variations over the season in professional soccer: A systematic review. Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part P: Journal of Sports Engineering and Technology. 2023;238(4):401-416.
paper.abstract: This systematic review summarized seasonal variation in acute:chronic workload ratio and training monotony among professional soccer players. PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and FECYT searches identified 27 studies with heterogeneous workload measures, calculation methods, periods, and outcomes.
paper.tldr: ACWR and training monotony vary substantially across the professional soccer season, but the literature does not support a universal injury-risk threshold. These measures are most defensible as descriptive workload context when their calculation and limitations are explicit.
paper.methods: The review followed PRISMA procedures and screened 225 records, retaining 27 studies. Extracted outcomes included different internal and external workload variables, ACWR calculations, monotony estimates, seasonal phases, and injury comparisons.
paper.findings: Reported ACWR and monotony values varied across preseason, competitive congestion, and lower-load weeks. Methodological differences were large, and the reviewed data did not conclusively distinguish injured from non-injured players.
paper.limitations: Workload definitions, sensors, aggregation windows, mathematical models, durations, and injury outcomes differed markedly. Most evidence was observational, limiting causal interpretation and preventing a defensible universal cut point.
paper.practicalImplications: If ACWR or monotony is displayed, show the underlying load variable, calculation method, time window, and athlete context. Use the measures to support longitudinal discussion, not as autonomous injury alarms or proof that a workload caused an injury.
paper.athleteDev: Use workload ratios as one view of progression alongside absolute exposure, intensity distribution, availability, and athlete response. Programming decisions should remain anchored to the actual work completed and the adaptation being targeted.
paper.rtp: ACWR should not serve as a return-to-sport clearance threshold. Reconditioning progression requires tissue-specific capacity, symptoms, clinical findings, sport demands, and exposure tolerance in addition to workload history.

records.sourceFile: Do environmental tempeatures and altitudes affect physical outputs of elite soccer athletes in match conditions - A systematic review of the 'real world' studies.pdf

paper.citation: Draper G, Wright MD, Ishida A, Chesterton P, Portas MD, Atkinson G. Do environmental temperatures and altitudes affect physical outputs of elite football athletes in match conditions? A systematic review of the 'real world' studies. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022;7(1):81-92.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated real-world studies of temperature, heat, cold, and altitude effects on elite football match-running outputs. Twelve observational studies were included, using varied tracking systems, exposure definitions, competitions, and physical-performance measures.
paper.tldr: Environmental temperature and altitude can influence selected match outputs, but the direction and size of effects were inconsistent across 12 real-world studies. Treat weather and altitude as planning context rather than deterministic performance penalties.
paper.methods: The authors systematically searched for observational match studies in elite football codes that reported environmental exposure and physical outputs. Study quality and the direction of findings were reviewed narratively because measurement and outcome heterogeneity limited pooling.
paper.findings: Some studies reported lower high-intensity or total running output in hotter conditions or at altitude, while others found minimal or different effects. Match context, tactics, opposition, pacing, acclimatization, and measurement choices likely contributed to the inconsistency.
paper.limitations: Only 12 heterogeneous real-world studies were available. Environmental categories, tracking technology, competitions, and outcomes differed, and uncontrolled match factors prevent strong causal estimates.
paper.practicalImplications: Use forecast temperature, humidity, and altitude to inform travel, acclimatization, hydration, warm-up, recovery, and substitution planning. Avoid forecasting an exact performance decrement from a single environmental threshold.
paper.athleteDev: Build environmental tolerance progressively when competition conditions warrant it and monitor individual responses. Preserve technical and tactical objectives while adjusting exposure and recovery support to the actual setting.
paper.rtp: Environmental load may change the cost of a return-to-participation session, especially after illness or deconditioning. Adjust exposure conservatively, but do not use this review as a standalone clearance or acclimatization protocol.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and performance after patellar fracture in American professional sports - A case-control cohort analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Moore BP, Hackl CM, Kneedler SC, Weiss WM. Return to play and performance after patellar fracture in American professional sports: A case-control cohort analysis. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2025;53(1):86-96.
paper.abstract: This retrospective case-control cohort study identified patellar fractures in NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL athletes from public reports and archives spanning 1965-2021. Return, playing volume, and sport-specific performance were assessed against preinjury levels and matched controls for two seasons after return.
paper.tldr: Twenty-nine of 41 professional athletes returned after patellar fracture, averaging 217 days. Playing volume commonly fell in the first season and approached baseline in the second, but the public-record design and missing fracture details make individual prognosis and treatment comparisons uncertain.
paper.methods: Forty-one professional athletes with an isolated patellar fracture were identified from public sources. Performance scores, playing time, and games were compared across the preinjury season and two post-return seasons, including matched-control analyses and operative versus nonoperative descriptions.
paper.findings: The return-to-play rate was 71% with a mean 217-day absence. Overall playing volume declined in year one and recovered toward baseline in year two; operative cases recovered performance by year two in this cohort, while year-one performance remained below matched controls.
paper.limitations: The study relied on retrospective public records, included a small multi-league sample, and used non-equivalent sport performance metrics. Fracture pattern, operative technique, rehabilitation details, and clinical decision criteria were unavailable, so treatment superiority cannot be inferred.
paper.practicalImplications: Set expectations around a potentially prolonged return and a staged restoration of playing volume after return. Use the cohort as a broad benchmark, not an athlete-specific timeline or evidence that one treatment strategy is better.
paper.athleteDev: Plan beyond the clearance date: the first season back may require deliberate exposure management, while performance volume may continue recovering into a second season. Coordinate strength, skill, and competition-load progression across disciplines.
paper.rtp: Return decisions should be individualized to healing, knee function, strength and power, sport-specific capacity, symptoms, and risk tolerance. The 217-day average and 71% return rate are descriptive professional-sport benchmarks, not clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Evening smartphone exposure impairs sleep quality and next-day performance in elite soccer players - A randomized controlled trial.pdf

paper.citation: Dridi N, Souissi MA, Dridi R, et al. Evening smartphone exposure impairs sleep quality and next-day performance in elite soccer players: A randomized controlled trial. Biology of Sport. 2026;43:227-242.
paper.abstract: This randomized crossover trial compared five nights of two-hour pre-bed smartphone use with magazine reading in 16 elite male soccer players. Sleep measures and morning and afternoon cognitive and physical performance tests were collected, separated by a one-week washout.
paper.tldr: Five nights of extended pre-bed smartphone use worsened sleep and selected next-day cognitive and physical outcomes in 16 elite male soccer players. A device-free wind-down period is reasonable, but the unusually large effects and very small, short study require replication.
paper.methods: Sixteen elite male players completed smartphone and control conditions in randomized crossover order. The smartphone condition involved two hours of use before bedtime; sleep duration, latency, efficiency, sleepiness, reaction time, jumping, and reactive agility were assessed across the intervention.
paper.findings: Smartphone exposure reduced total sleep time and efficiency, increased sleep latency and sleepiness, and worsened selected reaction-time, jumping, and reactive-agility outcomes, with several afternoon effects after five nights.
paper.limitations: The sample was very small, male, and limited to elite soccer; exposure lasted only five nights and participant blinding was impossible. Several reported effect sizes were unusually large, and behavior, content, light exposure, and expectancy may not be separable.
paper.practicalImplications: A consistent device-free period before bed is a low-cost sleep-support option, especially during demanding schedules. Monitor whether the strategy improves the individual athlete's sleep and daytime function rather than enforcing the study's exact duration as a universal rule.
paper.athleteDev: Include evening screen habits in sleep education and travel or competition routines. Focus on repeatable behavior change and athlete-specific response rather than framing all smartphone use as equally harmful.
paper.rtp: Sleep hygiene can support recovery and decision-making during rehabilitation, but smartphone restriction is not a return-to-sport criterion and cannot substitute for clinical or performance readiness measures.

records.sourceFile: Professional football (soccer) training and recovery - A longitudinal study on the effects of weekly conditioning session and workload variables.pdf

paper.citation: Curzi D, Amatori S, Silvestri F, et al. Professional football training and recovery: A longitudinal study on the effects of weekly conditioning session and workload variables. PLOS ONE. 2024;19(9):e0310036.
paper.abstract: This longitudinal study examined salivary testosterone and cortisol responses in 24 professional soccer players during comparable microcycles in the first and second halves of a season. Seven- and 28-day GPS workloads were related to hormonal measures collected before, after, and 24 hours after an MD-5 conditioning session.
paper.tldr: Later-season hormonal profiles were less favorable, and higher chronic workload was associated with a lower testosterone-to-cortisol ratio in one professional club. The findings are contextual correlations, not evidence that salivary hormones diagnose readiness or that workload caused the changes.
paper.methods: Twenty-four professional players were sampled at two seasonal time points. Salivary cortisol and testosterone were collected around an MD-5 session, while GPS total and high-intensity distance over the previous 7 and 28 days represented acute and chronic external workload.
paper.findings: Pretraining testosterone decreased and cortisol increased at the second time point. Chronic load correlated with cortisol and the testosterone-to-cortisol ratio more than acute load, suggesting accumulated seasonal context was related to the measured hormonal response.
paper.limitations: The cohort came from one club, attrition reduced available observations, and only two comparable microcycles were sampled. Hormonal measures are variable, the analyses were correlational, and ratio-based workload descriptors carry known limitations.
paper.practicalImplications: Interpret hormonal data, if collected, as one contextual trend alongside workload, sleep, wellness, performance, and clinical information. Avoid individual readiness labels or program changes from a single salivary value or testosterone-to-cortisol ratio.
paper.athleteDev: Review accumulated load and recovery response across the season, not just the most recent week. Adjust programming through converging evidence from exposure, athlete response, and performance rather than a hormone-only decision rule.
paper.rtp: Neither salivary hormones nor acute:chronic workload ratios should determine clearance. They may add context during reconditioning but require clinical, functional, and sport-specific readiness evidence.

records.sourceFile: Combining evidence and practice to optimize neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport - A systematic review and Delphi-consensus study.pdf

paper.citation: Fownes-Walpole M, Heyward O, Till K, et al. Combining evidence and practice to optimise neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport: A systematic review and Delphi-consensus study. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;59(15):1027-1042.
paper.abstract: This two-part consensus statement combined a systematic review of 21 neck-training studies with a three-round Delphi process involving 18 international experts. The work produced 57 consensus statements across assessment, programming, implementation, and monitoring topics intended to guide neck training for head-acceleration mitigation.
paper.tldr: The paper offers a practical expert-informed framework for neck training in collision, combat, and motor sport, but intervention evidence was too heterogeneous for quantitative efficacy estimates. Consensus on programming is not proof that a protocol reduces head acceleration or injury.
paper.methods: Four databases were searched through September 2024, with study quality assessed using modified Downs and Black and GRADE approaches. Findings informed three Delphi rounds with 18 experts, and statements meeting the prespecified agreement threshold were retained.
paper.findings: Twenty-one heterogeneous intervention studies were reviewed and 57 statements reached consensus. The resulting guidance emphasized individualized assessment, progressive multi-directional neck training, sport integration, technique, monitoring, and practitioner collaboration.
paper.limitations: Interventions, participants, outcomes, and measurement methods were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis, and much of the evidence was low certainty. Delphi agreement reflects expert judgment and does not establish causal reduction in head acceleration, concussion, or long-term brain-health risk.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the consensus as a structured implementation checklist while monitoring athlete tolerance, neck capacity, technique, and sport exposure. Keep claims proportional: the framework guides programming but does not guarantee fewer head impacts or injuries.
paper.athleteDev: Develop neck strength and control progressively across relevant directions and contraction types, integrated with whole-body collision or contact preparation. Individualize loading by training age, sport demands, symptoms, and technical competence.
paper.rtp: This is primarily preventive programming evidence, not a concussion return-to-sport protocol. Neck training should only be introduced within appropriate clinical guidance and cannot replace symptom, neurological, exertional, and sport-specific progression criteria.

records.sourceFile: A little pepper-upper - Systematic review of randomized controlled studies on capsaicinoids, capsinoids, and exercise performance.pdf

paper.citation: Sukan-Karaçağıl B, Akbulut G, Açar Y, Demirkoparan M. A little pepper-upper? Systematic review of randomized controlled studies on capsaicinoids, capsinoids, and exercise performance. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2023;33(5):291-301.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated randomized placebo-controlled human studies of capsaicinoid or capsinoid supplementation and exercise performance. Five databases were searched, risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool, and 19 trials were synthesized qualitatively.
paper.tldr: Ten of 19 randomized trials reported a positive performance outcome, with more apparent signal in resistance exercise than endurance exercise. Heterogeneous compounds, doses, outcomes, and incomplete safety reporting do not support a blanket supplement recommendation.
paper.methods: The review followed PRISMA procedures and searched PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library. Nineteen randomized placebo-controlled trials met inclusion criteria and were evaluated qualitatively because protocols and outcomes varied.
paper.findings: Ten studies reported positive performance effects, with the pattern appearing more frequently in resistance exercise. Findings were inconsistent across endurance and other exercise modes, and a pooled effect estimate was not produced.
paper.limitations: Compounds, doses, timing, participant training status, exercise tests, and outcomes were heterogeneous. Adverse effects were inconsistently reported, no meta-analysis was performed, and long-term effectiveness and safety remain uncertain.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat capsaicinoids and capsinoids as an unresolved, protocol-dependent supplement question. Any consideration requires dietitian and medical review of product quality, dose, gastrointestinal tolerance, interactions, and applicable sport rules.
paper.athleteDev: The evidence is not strong enough to build routine performance programming around these supplements. Prioritize established nutrition, training, and recovery practices before considering an individualized monitored trial.
paper.rtp: No return-to-sport benefit or rehabilitation protocol was established. Supplement use should not influence clearance or substitute for recovery milestones.

records.sourceFile: Effects of low-level laser therapy on muscular performance and soreness recovery in athletes - A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.pdf

paper.citation: Luo WT, Lee CJ, Tam KW, Huang TW. Effects of low-level laser therapy on muscular performance and soreness recovery in athletes: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Sports Health. 2022;14(5):687-693.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined low-level laser therapy before exercise in physically active athletes. PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library searches through December 2020 identified 24 randomized or crossover studies reporting muscular performance, soreness, or recovery biomarkers.
paper.tldr: Low-level laser therapy improved selected lower-limb strength follow-ups and some soreness or biomarker outcomes across 24 studies. Protocol heterogeneity and study limitations mean the therapy remains promising rather than an established standard recovery intervention.
paper.methods: Randomized controlled and crossover studies were pooled where outcomes and follow-up periods allowed. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane methods, and analyses examined strength, repetitions, oxygen kinetics, soreness, creatine kinase, interleukin-6, and oxidative-stress markers.
paper.findings: Preexercise therapy was associated with improved lower-limb strength at several follow-ups and reductions in selected soreness and biomarker outcomes. Trends were also reported for repetition performance and oxygen kinetics, but effects varied by outcome and protocol.
paper.limitations: Laser wavelength, dose, application site, timing, muscle group, exercise task, follow-up, and study quality varied. The authors noted that a definite therapeutic effect was not established and called for larger, more robust trials.
paper.practicalImplications: If used, document the exact device, wavelength, dose, site, and timing and evaluate whether the athlete experiences a meaningful benefit. Do not assume that findings from one protocol transfer to another device or recovery problem.
paper.athleteDev: Low-level laser therapy may be considered an adjunct around demanding training, but it should not displace load planning, sleep, nutrition, or progressive physical preparation with stronger foundations.
paper.rtp: The evidence does not establish low-level laser therapy as a return-to-sport milestone. It may be an adjunct within rehabilitation when clinically appropriate, while readiness remains based on tissue, symptoms, function, exposure, and sport demands.

records.sourceFile: Impact of melatonin supplementation on sports performance and circulating biomarkers in highly trained athletes - A systematic review of randomized controlled trials.pdf

paper.citation: Celorrio San Miguel AM, Roche E, Herranz-López M, Celorrio San Miguel M, Mielgo-Ayuso J, Fernández-Lázaro D. Impact of melatonin supplementation on sports performance and circulating biomarkers in highly trained athletes: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2024;16(7):1011.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined controlled trials of melatonin supplementation in highly trained athletes, focusing on performance and circulating health biomarkers. Searches of Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus through February 2024 yielded 21 studies using doses from 5 to 100 mg.
paper.tldr: Melatonin was associated with improvements in selected oxidative-stress, inflammatory, muscle-damage, and metabolic biomarkers across 21 controlled trials. Direct performance benefit remains unresolved, and the wide 5-100 mg dosing range prevents a simple athlete recommendation.
paper.methods: The review followed PRISMA procedures and applied modified McMaster, PEDro, and Cochrane appraisal tools. Twenty-one controlled trials in highly trained athletes were synthesized across varied exercise protocols, timing strategies, doses, and biomarker panels.
paper.findings: Selected antioxidant, inflammatory, liver, muscle-damage, glycemic, lipid, creatinine, hematological, and hormonal outcomes improved in some trials. The authors concluded that direct performance-enhancing efficiency still requires assessment and that any benefit may be indirect through health biomarkers.
paper.limitations: Dose, timing, exercise protocol, participant samples, biomarker selection, and study quality were heterogeneous. Biomarker changes do not necessarily represent meaningful performance or recovery improvement, and the review does not establish an optimal or universally safe dose.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not translate biomarker findings into routine high-dose supplementation. Melatonin decisions should be individualized with medical and nutrition oversight, attention to timing, side effects, product quality, sleep goals, and applicable regulations.
paper.athleteDev: Melatonin is not established as a direct performance enhancer. Address schedule, light exposure, sleep opportunity, and behavioral sleep practices before treating supplementation as the primary solution.
paper.rtp: No return-to-sport criterion or rehabilitation benefit was established. Melatonin may be considered for a specific sleep-related indication under appropriate oversight, but not as evidence of readiness.

records.sourceFile: Does longer-muscle length resistance training cause greater longitudinal growth in humans - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Wolf M, Androulakis Korakakis P, Roberts MD, et al. Does longer-muscle length resistance training cause greater longitudinal growth in humans? A systematic review. Sports Medicine and Health Science. 2026;8(1):34-42.
paper.abstract: This systematic review compared resistance training at longer versus shorter muscle lengths in healthy adults when studies measured both muscle size and fascicle length. Eight interventions totaling 120 participants met the criteria and were narratively synthesized.
paper.tldr: Training at longer muscle lengths generally favored muscle hypertrophy and may favor fascicle-length change, but the evidence is mixed. No included study directly measured serial sarcomere number, so sarcomerogenesis remains a proposed mechanism rather than a demonstrated human adaptation.
paper.methods: Google Scholar, PubMed/MEDLINE, and Scopus were searched in February 2024, supplemented by citation searching and author knowledge. Eligible studies lasted at least four weeks, compared longer- with shorter-muscle-length training, and measured muscle size and fascicle length.
paper.findings: Across eight studies and 120 participants, longer-muscle-length training generally produced greater overall hypertrophy and sometimes greater estimated fascicle-length change. Results were mixed, and the structural basis of the observed changes remains unresolved.
paper.limitations: No study directly estimated serial sarcomere number, and all but one used questionable linear-extrapolation methods for fascicle length. Samples and exercises were limited, results were narratively synthesized, and applicability to highly trained athletes is uncertain.
paper.practicalImplications: Include well-tolerated loading at longer muscle lengths when hypertrophy is a goal, but progress range and load to the athlete and exercise. Avoid promising a unique sarcomerogenesis effect that current human measurements cannot confirm.
paper.athleteDev: Longer-muscle-length resistance exercise can be one programming option for hypertrophy rather than a replacement for sound volume, effort, progression, and exercise selection. Monitor tolerance because the review did not establish one universal protocol.
paper.rtp: The review studied healthy-adult hypertrophy, not injured-athlete return. Longer-length loading may be introduced during later rehabilitation when tissue tolerance and clinical goals support it, but it is not a clearance standard.
